passages.t: The sons of God and the daughters of men
passages.happening:
People multiply on the earth, and daughters are born. “The sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose” (verse 2).

Then the LORD sets a limit: “My Spirit will not contend with man forever, for he is mortal; his days shall be 120 years” (verse 3).

The passage ends with the Nephilim. They “were on the earth in those days”, when the sons of God had children by the daughters of men. Their children “became the mighty men of old, men of renown” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
These four verses are among the strangest in the Bible, and they were strange to ancient readers too. Many peoples around Israel told stories of gods who had children with humans, and of heroes born from them. Kings often claimed a god as their father.

Notice the words ‘saw’, ‘beautiful’ (literally ‘good’) and ‘took’. They are the same three steps as in the garden, where the woman saw that the tree was good and took (3:6). Once again someone sees, desires and takes, crossing a line God had set.

The ‘mighty men of old, men of renown’ sound like the famous heroes of other nations' stories. Genesis gives them one sentence and no praise. Their fame is part of the problem, not the answer. Soon the story will show what this world of famous, mighty men was really like: ‘full of violence’ (verse 11).

No one is sure what the name Nephilim means. They appear once more, when Israel's frightened spies say they saw Nephilim in Canaan (Numbers 13:33).
passages.later:
The phrase ‘sons of God’ appears elsewhere in the Old Testament for heavenly beings. In Job, “the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD” (Job 1:6).

Two New Testament letters speak of angels who sinned. Jude writes of “the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling” (Jude 1:6). Peter says God “did not spare the angels when they sinned” and in the next verse speaks of the flood (2 Peter 2:4-5). Many readers think both letters have Genesis 6 in mind; others do not.

Jesus says that in the resurrection people “will neither marry nor be given in marriage,” but “will be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30). Readers on every side of this question weigh those words.
passages.hard:
Who were the ‘sons of God’? Christians and Jews have read these verses in three main ways, and each has good reasons and real difficulties.

Angels. Many early Jewish and Christian readers took the sons of God to be heavenly beings who crossed the line between heaven and earth. Job uses the phrase for heavenly beings, and Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may refer to this story. The difficulty: Jesus says angels do not marry, and the text does not explain how spirits could have children.

The line of Seth. From about the fourth century, most Christian teachers, Augustine among them, read the sons of God as the faithful family of Seth and the daughters of men as the family of Cain. The sin was God's people marrying those who did not worship him. The difficulty: the text never calls Seth's family ‘sons of God’, and it says ‘men’, not ‘Cain’.

Rulers. Some ancient Jewish translations read the phrase as ‘the sons of the great ones’ or ‘the sons of the rulers’: powerful kings who called themselves sons of gods and took any women they wanted. The difficulty: the Bible rarely uses the phrase this way.

These notes take no side. On each reading the point is the same: a boundary was crossed, power and pride grew, and God set a limit.

What does ‘120 years’ mean? Some read it as a new limit on the length of a human life. Others read it as the time left before the flood would come. Both are possible.
passages.asks: Seeing, wanting and taking: the same pattern as the garden. Ask where you see something good and take it in a way God has not given. And notice which people this world called famous. Ask whose ‘renown’ you admire, and whether God would admire it too.

passages.t: God's grief, and one man's favor
passages.happening:
“Then the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time” (verse 5).

The next words are startling: “And the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart” (verse 6). He resolves to blot out human beings and animals from the face of the earth, “for I am grieved that I have made them” (verse 7).

Then one sentence turns the story: “Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Verse 5 is one of the strongest statements about human sin in the Bible. It is not one bad act. It is every inclination, of every thought, all the time. The word ‘inclination’ (yetser) comes from the verb used of a potter shaping clay (2:7). The hearts God shaped have shaped themselves for evil.

The word for God's grief in verse 6 comes from the same Hebrew root as the ‘pain’ of the woman's childbearing and the man's toil in 3:16-17. The pain sin brought to people, God now feels himself.

And the word ‘regretted’ (nacham) is the same verb Lamech used when he named Noah for ‘comfort’ (5:29). The man named for comfort is born into the world over which God grieves.

In Hebrew, Noah's name and the word for ‘favor’ use the same two letters, in reverse order. A listener would hear the turn: Noah, and then favor. The word ‘favor’ is the Old Testament's word for grace, kindness that is given, not earned.
passages.later:
The same strange pairing comes again in 1 Samuel 15. God says, “I regret that I have made Saul king” (1 Samuel 15:11). A few verses later Samuel says that God “does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man” (1 Samuel 15:29). And at the end of the chapter, “the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel” (1 Samuel 15:35). The writer puts both in the same chapter, so he did not think they cancel each other.

Elsewhere God's grief over his people is fierce and tender: “How could I give you up, O Ephraim?” (Hosea 11:8). Paul warns, “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30). The God of the Bible can be grieved.

Ezekiel says what God wants instead of judgment: “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).
passages.hard:
‘The LORD regretted that He had made man.’ Can God regret, if he knows everything and ‘does not change His mind’ (1 Samuel 15:29)? Christians have answered in more than one way.

Many teachers through history have said that the Bible here speaks of God in human terms, so that people can understand. God's purpose does not change; but from where we stand, his turn from blessing to judgment looks like a change of mind. On this reading the verse shows how seriously God takes sin, without saying that he was surprised.

Others stress that the God of the Bible is personal, not a cold machine. He truly responds to what people do and truly feels grief. On this reading God's purpose and character never change, but his response to people does, as Jeremiah says: if a nation turns from evil, God will ‘relent of the disaster’ he had planned (Jeremiah 18:8).

Many hold both together. God does not change in his character, his promises or his purpose. And he is not unmoved by the wickedness of the world. 1 Samuel 15 sets the two side by side, and these notes do too.

What the verse plainly shows is that judgment does not come from a God who does not care. It comes from a God whose heart is grieved.
passages.asks: The first feeling God shows in this chapter is not anger but grief. Ask whether you picture God as cold toward the world's evil, or as grieved by it. Then notice Noah: grace found in a dark world. Ask where you need to receive favor you cannot earn.

passages.happening:
A new section begins: “This is the account of Noah” (verse 9). Noah is “a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah walked with God.” He has three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth (verse 10).

But the earth “was corrupt in the sight of God, and full of violence” (verse 11). God looks, and sees that “all living creatures on the earth had corrupted their ways” (verse 12).

God tells Noah what he will do. “The end of all living creatures has come before Me, because through them the earth is full of violence” (verse 13). He says he will destroy them along with the earth.
passages.hearers:
The key word of these verses is shachat, to spoil, corrupt or destroy. The earth was ‘corrupt’, all flesh had ‘corrupted’ its ways, and God says he will ‘destroy’ it. It is the same verb each time. The flood is not God wrecking a healthy world. It is God bringing to an end a world that people had already ruined.

The other key word is chamas, violence. It means more than force. It covers bloodshed, injustice and the strong crushing the weak. Later prophets use it for oppression in Israel's own cities. Cain killed one brother; Lamech boasted of killing; now violence fills the earth.

The first hearers knew other flood stories. In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis, the gods send a flood because people have grown too many and too noisy, and they keep the chief god awake. Genesis gives a very different reason. God does not judge because people are noisy. He judges because they are violent and have spoiled his good world.

Noah ‘walked with God’, like Enoch (5:24). Blameless does not mean sinless; the story will show his failings (9:20-21). It means he was whole-hearted toward God in a generation that was not.
passages.later:
Peter calls Noah “a preacher of righteousness” (2 Peter 2:5). Hebrews says, “By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family” (Hebrews 11:7).

Jesus uses Noah's day as a warning about his own return: “As it was in the days of Noah, so will it be at the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:37). His point is not that people were unusually wicked, but that they were unready. They were “eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark” (Matthew 24:38).

Peter adds that God's delay is mercy. The Lord “is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).
passages.hard:
This chapter tells of judgment on the whole earth. It is right to feel its weight. The text does not hide that people and animals will die. These notes will not hide it either.

Three things help a reader hold it honestly. First, the reason is given: violence and the ruin of the world, not a whim. Second, God grieves before he acts (verse 6). Third, he makes a way through: an ark, and later a promise never to do this again (9:11).

A word for younger readers. This story can be frightening. The flood is not a story about God wanting to hurt children, and it is not a warning that the next storm is aimed at you. God himself promised that a flood like this will never happen again (9:11), and he gave the rainbow to remember it. If the story worries you, talk about it with a parent or someone you trust.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: God saw violence and called it ruin. Ask where violence, in word or deed, has been made normal around you, and whether it has become normal in you. Then look at Noah: one man walking with God when no one else was. Ask whether you need others' approval to do what is right.

passages.happening:
God tells Noah to build an ark of “gopher wood”, with rooms, coated with pitch inside and out (verse 14). It is to be 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide and 30 cubits high (verse 15), with a roof, a door in the side, and three decks (verse 16).

God says he will bring floodwaters to destroy every creature that has the breath of life (verse 17). “But I will establish My covenant with you,” he says, and Noah will go into the ark with his wife, his sons and their wives (verse 18).

Noah is to bring two of every kind of creature, male and female, “to keep them alive” (verses 19-20), and food for them all (verse 21). “So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
A cubit was the length of a man's forearm, from elbow to fingertip, often reckoned at about 18 inches (45 centimeters). On that measure the ark was roughly 450 feet long, 75 feet wide and 45 feet high (about 137 by 23 by 14 meters). It was not a ship to sail but a great box to float, with no sail or rudder. In the Gilgamesh flood story, the boat is usually read as a cube, its sides equal. The ark's long, narrow shape is very different.

‘Gopher wood’ is named nowhere else, and no one knows for sure what tree it was. Cypress is a common guess. Pitch, a kind of tar, was used in Mesopotamia to seal boats.

The word for ‘ark’, tevah, is used in only one other story in the Bible: the basket in which baby Moses was placed on the Nile. His mother “coated it with tar and pitch” (Exodus 2:3). Both are boxes that carry a chosen life through deadly water.

Verse 18 holds the first ‘covenant’ in the Bible, a binding promise that creates a lasting bond. Before the rain falls, God promises to keep Noah and his family. The animals are saved too, ‘to keep them alive’. God's care reaches his creatures, not only people.
passages.later:
Peter sees the ark as a picture of rescue: “In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water” (1 Peter 3:20). He links it with baptism, which saves “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 3:21).

The covenant promised here is made in chapter 9 with Noah and every living creature (Genesis 9:9-10). It is the first of the great covenants that run through the Bible, to Abraham, to Israel at Sinai, to David, and the new covenant Jesus spoke of at his last supper (Luke 22:20).

Hebrews says Noah built “in godly fear” (Hebrews 11:7). His obedience was not a feeling. It was years of work on something no one around him could yet see the need for.
passages.asks: ‘Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.’ Ask what God has already made plain to you that you have not yet done. Then notice that God made a promise before the rain began. Ask what promise of God you need to hold on to before you can see how the story ends.
